title: Security & Threat Modeling
subtitle: Identify assets, attacker capabilities, trust boundaries, and controls before choosing security products
objectives: Model concrete threats against assets and trust boundaries
Apply least privilege and defense in depth
Protect secrets and sensitive data through their complete lifecycle
Design abuse controls and security evidence

lessons.title: Model the attacker and the asset

exercises.title: A threat model connects an asset, an attacker capability, and an attack path
exercises.body: Begin with the asset to protect, who may attack it, what that actor can control, and which boundary the input crosses. A useful threat states a plausible path and consequence, allowing a control to block, detect, or limit that path.
exercises.note: Calling a component secure is not a threat model. Name the operation, identity, data, boundary, and failure consequence.

exercises.prompt: An upload service trusts the client-supplied filename and writes it directly under `/uploads`. Prevent a filename such as `../../config` from escaping the assigned object namespace.
choices: Reject filenames containing one known string
Generate an opaque object key and store the display name as metadata
Run the upload service as database administrator
choiceFeedback: A blacklist misses alternative encodings and path forms.
An opaque server-side key removes the client string from the storage path.
Additional privilege increases the damage of a successful escape.
exercises.beforeStatus: BOUNDARY FAILURE · client path selects server file location
exercises.afterStatus: BOUNDARY ENFORCED · server key selects location · display name is data
exercises.result: Untrusted presentation text no longer controls a storage path
exercises.why: The service assigns the storage identifier and treats the original filename as untrusted metadata. Canonicalization and allowlisted content rules remain necessary wherever external input influences a path, parser, command, or downstream request.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: An upload service trusts the client-supplied filename and writes it directly under `/uploads`. Prevent a filename such as `../../config` from escaping the assigned object namespace. Place Upload service, Object storage. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Client filename → Upload service; Upload service → Object storage. That topology is the evidence for the answer: The service assigns the storage identifier and treats the original filename as untrusted metadata. Canonicalization and allowlisted content rules remain necessary wherever external input influences a path, parser, command, or downstream request.

exercises.prompt: Which questions make a threat concrete? Select all.
choices: Which cloud logo looks most secure?
exercises.why: Assets, attacker capabilities, and trust boundaries define a testable attack path. A vendor choice can implement a control only after the threat and required property are clear.

exercises.prompt: Match each security property to the failure it prevents.
exercises.why: Confidentiality restricts reading, integrity restricts undetected modification, and availability preserves required service. One incident can violate several properties at once.

exercises.title: Least privilege limits what one compromised component can do
exercises.body: Grant each workload only the actions and resources required for its current job. Scope permissions by operation, resource, environment, and lifetime so a compromised worker cannot automatically reach unrelated data or administrative functions.
exercises.note: Least privilege reduces blast radius; it does not prevent the initial compromise or replace monitoring and recovery.

exercises.prompt: An image-resize worker uses one account with read, write, delete, and payment-database access. Restrict the identity to its actual data path.
choices: Keep the administrator key but hide its filename
Grant read on source objects and write on one result prefix
Give every worker a separate administrator key
choiceFeedback: Obscurity does not change the permissions available after compromise.
The scoped identity contains compromise to the worker's required object operations.
Separate administrator keys improve attribution but preserve excessive authority.
exercises.beforeStatus: BLAST RADIUS · worker compromise reaches storage deletion and payments
exercises.afterStatus: BLAST RADIUS · source read + result write in one object prefix
exercises.result: Workload permissions now match the worker's responsibility
exercises.why: A short-lived workload identity with resource-scoped operations limits both exposure time and reachable assets. Permission review must also remove obsolete grants when the worker's role changes.

exercises.prompt: Complete the system for this case: An image-resize worker uses one account with read, write, delete, and payment-database access. Restrict the identity to its actual data path. Place Worker identity, Image prefix. Then connect the components in the direction that requests, data, or events move.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Worker identity → Image prefix. That topology is the evidence for the answer: A short-lived workload identity with resource-scoped operations limits both exposure time and reachable assets. Permission review must also remove obsolete grants when the worker's role changes.

exercises.prompt: Why is encrypting a database while storing its decryption key beside it under the same unrestricted service account insufficient?
choices: The same compromise can retrieve both ciphertext and key, so the trust boundary did not change
exercises.why: Encryption protects against threats that obtain the stored bytes without equivalent key access. Separating key authority, auditing use, and narrowing decrypt permission create a distinct boundary that the attacker must also cross.

steps: Allow consumers to read both old and new versions during a bounded overlap
Deploy consumers that prefer the new version
Verify successful use and rollback readiness
exercises.why: A bounded overlap prevents an instantaneous fleet-wide dependency. Consumers move first, evidence confirms adoption, and revocation closes the old credential after rollback is no longer required.

exercises.title: Security controls need prevention, detection, and recovery paths
exercises.body: Preventive controls block known unsafe operations, detective controls record and alert on suspicious behavior, and recovery controls restore safe service after compromise. A design that only rejects requests cannot explain how an undetected breach is found or contained.
exercises.note: Audit events must identify the principal, action, resource, result, and trustworthy time source without recording secrets unnecessarily.

exercises.prompt: Build an account-protection path that can block abusive sign-in attempts and preserve evidence.
exercises.why: Admission controls slow automated abuse before expensive verification, while a protected audit trail preserves sign-in outcomes for detection and investigation. Neither control replaces strong credential verification.

exercises.prompt: Build the end-to-end path required by this scenario: Build an account-protection path that can block abusive sign-in attempts and preserve evidence.
exercises.why: The completed diagram contains these directed flows: Sign-in request → Risk-aware rate limit; Risk-aware rate limit → Identity service; Identity service → Append-only security audit. That topology is the evidence for the answer: Admission controls slow automated abuse before expensive verification, while a protected audit trail preserves sign-in outcomes for detection and investigation. Neither control replaces strong credential verification.

exercises.prompt: Which fields belong in a privileged-action audit event? Select all.
exercises.why: An audit event needs enough context to reconstruct who attempted which action on what resource and whether it succeeded. Recording a password creates a new credential exposure and is unnecessary evidence.

exercises.prompt: A public login endpoint sees credential-stuffing attacks from rotating addresses. Choose the admission-control emphasis.
exercises.rightLabel: Risk signals across account, device, network, and behavior
exercises.why: Rotating addresses defeat an IP-only quota. Combining account, device, network, and behavioral signals raises attacker cost, while controls need thresholds and recovery paths that limit false lockouts for legitimate users.

exercises.prompt: A webhook tester fetches any URL supplied by a user. An attacker submits a cloud metadata address reachable only from the server. What threat is this?
choices: Server-side request forgery across a trust boundary
exercises.why: The attacker makes the trusted server initiate a request to an internal destination they cannot reach directly. URL validation, network egress policy, and metadata-service protections constrain that capability.
